_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: To add women: who are obligated in reading the Megilla, and are fit to read it and to fulfill the obligation of men.
tosafot:a1.1: To add women: who are obligated in reading the Megilla, and fit to read it and to fulfill the obligation of men; so [Rashi’s] wording. But the Halakhot Gedolot did not rule so, and they bring a proof from the Tosefta, whose wording is: “Everyone is obligated in reading the Megilla… A tumtum and a hermaphrodite are obligated, but they do not fulfill the obligation of the many. A hermaphrodite fulfills the obligation of his own kind but not of another kind. A tumtum fulfills the obligation neither of his own kind nor of another kind. One who is half-slave and half-free fulfills the obligation neither of his own kind nor of another kind. Women, slaves and minors are exempt from reading the Megilla.” Up to here the wording of the Tosefta. And the Halakhot Gedolot added: but they are obligated in hearing it, since all were in danger of being destroyed, killed and annihilated.
tosafot:a1.2: [Ruling:] Rabbi Yehoshua [ben Levi] would gather all the members of his household and read before them. Rabbi Yona, the father of Rabbi Menaḥem, would make a point of reading it before the women of his household, since all were in danger and all are obligated in hearing it. Up to here the wording of the Halakhot Gedolot. So one must explain here that women fulfill the obligation only of women, not of men, and “Everyone is obligated in reading the Megilla… to add women” [means: who can fulfill the obligation of other women]. And [the Gemara] could have said “to add a minor,” according to Rabbi Yehuda, who deems a minor fit, in the second chapter of Megilla (19b).
rashi:a2.1: Form a zimmun for themselves: three women, and likewise three slaves. But two women or two slaves do not join with [two] men, because men have something that women and slaves do not: women do not say “covenant” [in Grace after Meals], and slaves do not say “for our inheritance.”
tosafot:a2.1: Form a zimmun for themselves: three women, and likewise three slaves. But two women do not join with men, because men have something that women and slaves do not: women do not say “covenant,” and slaves do not say “the land that You gave as an inheritance to our fathers.” And one must say that this is permission for women to form a zimmun, but there is no obligation. Know this, since [the Gemara] cites it as support for the one who says in chapter Shelosha She’akhlu (Berakhot 45b) that women, if they wish to form a zimmun, may do so, since a hundred women are like two men; and if they were obligated, that would be difficult, since it says “if they wish to form a zimmun.” And on this our women have relied in not forming a zimmun.
tosafot:a3.1: To add a minor who knows to Whom one recites a blessing, as Rav Naḥman, etc.: and it is also said in Berakhot (48a): “The halakha is not in accordance with any of these statements, but in accordance with Rav Naḥman,” etc. Even so, we do not hold like him, but as Rabbi Yosei says in the Jerusalem Talmud: “Many times I ate with my father Ḥalafta and with Ḥavivi, and they did not count me for a zimmun until I had grown two hairs.”
rashi:a4.1: “Any man [ish ish]”: “when he has an issue out of his flesh,” etc. (Leviticus 15:2).
tosafot:a4.1: As it is taught: “Any man, when he has an issue,” etc. The reason [the Gemara] does not cite the mishna in chapter Yotzei Dofen (Niddah 43b), where we learned that a day-old baby becomes impure through ziva, is that the baraita explains more.
gershom:a1.1: Why does the verse state “man, man [ish ish]” twice, “when he has an issue out of his flesh”?
rashi:a7.1: From karet: this verse is written about one who enters the Temple while impure, and it makes him liable to karet. That is why “man” is written, to exclude a minor, who is not subject to punishment. But he is impure, and makes food and drink impure, like an adult.
tosafot:a7.1: To exclude a minor from karet: this verse is written about one who enters the Temple while impure, and it makes him liable to karet; that is why “man” is written, to exclude a minor, who is not subject to punishment, though he is impure and makes food and drink impure like an adult. One may wonder: why do I need a verse to exempt him, since we never find a minor punished? And it is likewise difficult in chapter Arba Mitot (Sanhedrin 52b): “A man who commits adultery” excludes a minor. There, though, one can say that [without the verse] he would be liable because of the woman’s disgrace, like the animal that was the object of bestiality. And perhaps here it was needed because it might enter your mind that, since he was included for impurity, he is liable to karet; it teaches us that he is not.
gershom:a2.1: To exclude a minor from karet: for impurity of the Temple and its consecrated items.
rashi:a10.1: “And the leper”: implies another leper, to include a woman.
tosafot:a10.1: “And the leper”: implies another leper, to include a woman. If so, why is “man” stated? For the matter below: “man” implies not a woman, and it does not refer to “he shall surely pronounce him impure,” since there even a woman [is impure], but to the verse below, which speaks of letting the hair grow and rending; so [Rashi’s] wording. And although “woman” is written regarding marks of the head and beard (Leviticus 13:29), we do not derive from there, since there it was needed [to teach] that although hair does not usually grow in a woman’s beard, she becomes impure. One might ask: why not derive a woman from “a person [adam],” which implies a woman just as it implies a minor, as it is written “and persons [nefesh adam]” (Numbers 31:35)? Since they are equal, let both be derived. One may answer: it might enter your mind that since a verse was needed to include a woman for marks of the [beard; the printed text reads “minor”], it follows that other marks do not render a woman impure unless from that verse. And it is difficult: [the Torah] should have included a woman from “a person,” used “man” to exclude a minor from letting the hair grow and rending, and “and the leper” to include a minor in impurity. One may answer that it is more reasonable to exclude a woman from letting the hair grow and rending, since that is a disgrace.
gershom:a3.1: When it says “leper,” there are two here: that is, “leper” means anyone who is a leper, whether man or woman. If so, why does the verse state “man”? For the matter below, “And the leper in whom the mark is”: a man lets his hair grow and rends [his garments], but a woman does not let her hair grow and does not rend. And if it is difficult: what need is there to include a woman from “leper,” when a woman is written explicitly regarding leprous marks, as it is written, “And a man or a woman, when there shall be in the skin of their flesh bright spots,” etc.? That is not difficult: that is a pure mark.
rashi:a11.1: If so, why is “man” stated? For the matter below: it implies a man and not a woman. It does not refer to “he shall surely pronounce him impure,” since there even a woman [is impure]; it refers to the verse below, which speaks of letting the hair grow and rending.
rashi:a12.1: “Everyone may inspect” and “everyone is fit to inspect” are one [teaching], and they are not taught together.
tosafot:a12.1: “Everyone may inspect” and “everyone is fit to inspect” are one [teaching], and they are not taught together.
gershom:a4.1: “Everyone may inspect leprous marks” and “everyone is fit to inspect” are one; but since they are not taught together, both are taught. And some say: “Everyone may inspect leprous marks” means everyone can inspect leprous marks although they are not expert; “and everyone is fit to inspect” means even though the verse made it depend on the priests. (The note ends with an abbreviation whose meaning is unclear.)
rashi:a12.2: Who is not expert: an Israelite Torah scholar goes and inspects with him and tells him, “Say: impure,” and he says it [the printed text reads “and he says pure”; Tosafot, quoting Rashi, read “he says impure”], since impurity and purity depend on the priest’s declaration. And so it is taught in Torat Kohanim.
rashi:a13.1: But didn’t the Master say: in the first chapter of Shevuot (6a).
tosafot:a13.1: But didn’t the Master say: in the first chapter of Shevuot (6a).
rashi:a13.2: Where they explain to him and he understands: the laws of leprous marks.
tosafot:a13.2: Where they explain to him and he understands: the laws of leprous marks. Who is not expert: a Torah scholar goes and inspects with him; he says “impure,” and [the priest] says “impure,” since impurity and purity depend on the priest’s declaration, and so it is taught in Torat Kohanim; so [Rashi’s] wording. And there in Torat Kohanim an Israelite is included from what is written, “or to one [of his sons the priests],” and we conclude there: since in the end it includes an Israelite, for what halakha is “priest” written? That impurity and purity come only from the mouth of a priest, so that even a foolish priest may inspect leprous marks. Although they explain to him and he understands, he is called a foolish priest, since on his own he is not expert. Another explanation: “they explain to him and he understands” here does not refer to the priest but to the learned Israelite who stands beside him. And if you say: obviously! What difference is there between being taught yesterday and being taught today? One may answer: although he is expert only in that one mark, he is fit to inspect.
gershom:a5.1: Where they explain to him and he understands: they tell him, “Go and see whether they are formed like such and such,” and he understands and sees.
rashi:a14.1: To sanctify: to mix living water with the ashes of the purification offering. The reason of the Rabbis and of Rabbi Yehuda is explained in tractate Yoma, chapter Taraf BaKalpi (Yoma 43a).
tosafot:a14.1: To sanctify: to mix living water with the ashes of the purification offering. The reason of Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis is explained in chapter Taraf BaKalpi (Yoma 43a).
gershom:a6.1: Everyone is fit to sanctify: to put the ashes of the purification offering into the water.
gershom:a7.1: Rabbi Yehuda deems a minor fit, etc.: their reasons are explained in tractate Yoma.
rashi:a15.1: One who is uncircumcised: whose brothers died as a result of circumcision.
gershom:a8.1: Uncircumcised: whose brothers died as a result of circumcision.
rashi:a15.2: Who sprinkled: purification water on the impure person.
rashi:a15.3: His sprinkling is valid: the reason is explained in Yevamot, chapter HaArel (72b): just as with one who immersed that day, who is unfit for teruma but fit for [the rites of] the red heifer.
tosafot:a15.1: One who is uncircumcised: whose brothers died as a result of circumcision. Who sprinkled purification water on the impure person, his sprinkling is valid: the reason is explained in Yevamot, chapter HaArel (72b): just as with one who immersed that day, who is unfit for teruma and fit for [the rites of] the red heifer. And [the Gemara] could have cited the baraita taught there that says this explicitly, but Rabbi Elazar’s statement is more familiar to everyone.
rashi:a16.1: There are two [mishnayot that say] “Everyone slaughters” in the first chapter of Ḥullin (2a and 15b).
tosafot:a16.1: There are two “Everyone slaughters” in the first chapter of Ḥullin (2a and 15b).
gershom:a9.1: Everyone slaughters: there are two “Everyone slaughters” in the first mishna of Shechitat Ḥullin.
gershom:a10.1: An apostate Jew: one who is an apostate with regard to one matter.
rashi:a17.1: Everyone can force others to ascend: in the last chapter of Ketubot (110b).
tosafot:a17.1: Everyone can force others to ascend: in Ketubot, the last chapter (110b).
rashi:b1.1: To add slaves: if he has a circumcised Canaanite slave to sell, and the slave wants him to sell him only in Eretz Yisrael, the master is forced to take him up [there].
tosafot:b1.1: To add slaves: if he has a circumcised Canaanite slave to sell, and the slave wants him to sell him only in Eretz Yisrael. And in Ketubot (110b) Rashi explained that he can take up [a Hebrew slave against the slave’s will]. And the Ri explained that the slave can compel [his master] to take him up, or else they must free him.
rashi:b1.2: From a pleasant residence: outside the Land.
rashi:b1.3: To a noxious residence: in Eretz Yisrael, and his wife cannot prevent him. And likewise from Eretz Yisrael to Jerusalem.
gershom:b1.1: To add from a pleasant residence to a noxious residence: even though he has a pleasant residence outside the Land and a noxious residence in Eretz Yisrael.
tosafot:b2.1: To add a slave who fled from outside the Land to the Land: according to the one who teaches slaves [explicitly], we would not have known this from the first clause, even by Rashi’s explanation that it speaks of Canaanite slaves whom he wants to sell, since [there] he does not remove the slave from his possession. Alternatively, since he fled, one might have penalized the slave so that he would not be freed. Alternatively, it might enter your mind that the first clause speaks of a master who regularly goes to Eretz Yisrael in any case.
gershom:b2.1: A slave who fled from outside the Land to the Land: his master cannot remove him from there.
tosafot:b3.1: From a pleasant residence outside the Land to a noxious residence in Eretz Yisrael, and his wife cannot prevent him, and likewise from Eretz Yisrael to Jerusalem; so [Rashi’s] wording. [The reason] that although the first clause taught “All may force others to ascend,” the latter clause teaches “But all may not remove,” is explained there in Ketubot (also there). And one cannot say [it comes] to add slaves, since regarding slaves there is no difference between the rest of Eretz Yisrael and Jerusalem.
gershom:b3.1: All may force others to ascend to Jerusalem, even though Jerusalem is a noxious residence, as we say in tractate Ketubot: From where [do we know] that living in large cities is hard? As it is stated: “And the people blessed all the men who willingly offered themselves [to dwell in Jerusalem].”
rashi:b4.1: [Obvious]: until now [the Gemara] expounded “everyone” as adding something; from here on it expounds those [teachings] that state “priests, Levites and Israelites,” and asks: obvious! If these are not obligated, who would be?
tosafot:b4.1: Everyone is obligated in sukka: until now [the Gemara] expounded “everyone” as adding something; from here on it expounds those that state “priests, Levites and Israelites,” and asks: obvious! If these are not obligated, who would be?
gershom:b4.1: [A later editor notes that the text seems to need: “And now he asks, wherever priests, Levites and Israelites are taught, to add what?”] Just as it says “Everyone may pledge valuations” [and means] priests, Levites and Israelites, so too for all these “everyone” that we learned he asks: “Everyone is obligated in sukka, priests, Levites and Israelites” — obvious! If these are not obligated, who is?
rashi:b5.1: And they are occupied with the service: and a man and his wife cannot reside in the sukka together, since they do not have relations with their wives, as the service of the Festival rests upon them; so say that they should not be obligated.
tosafot:b5.1: And they are occupied with the service: and a man and his wife cannot reside in the sukka together, since they do not have relations with their wives, as the service of the Festival rests upon them; so say that they should not be obligated. So [Rashi’s] wording. For on the reasoning that applies to travelers they cannot be exempted, [since that applies] only in the fields, not in a chamber of the Temple and the other places of the Temple. And [the Gemara] could equally have mentioned the Levites, who kept guard in twenty-one places in the Temple, as stated in the first chapter of Tamid (26a). So too we find below, regarding “Everyone is obligated to sound the shofar,” that it could have said priests and Levites were needed, since it also cites that Levites redeem at any time and sell at any time, and yet it mentions only priests.
gershom:b6.1: Also the sukka, a man and his wife: and priests need to be apart [from their wives], since they must perform the service on the Festival.
rashi:b6.1: It teaches us: that although they cannot [fulfill] “as you dwell,” to the extent that they can, they are obligated: at the time of service they are exempt; when it is not the time of service they are obligated.
tosafot:b6.1: It teaches us: that although they cannot [fulfill] the manner of dwelling, to the extent that they can, they are obligated: at the time of service they are exempt; when it is not the time of service they are obligated.
gershom:b5.1: Also the sukka, by day and by night. And these priests, since they cannot sit in it by day because they are busy with the service, should be exempt at night as well; it teaches us [that they are not].
tosafot:b8.1: These priests, since diverse kinds are permitted to them, etc.: the Ri of Orléans asked: then women should not be obligated [in the prohibition of] diverse kinds, since they are not included in “You shall make yourself twisted cords”! One may answer: the verse equated a woman to a man. And as for what is said in chapter Elu Ovrin (Pesaḥim 43b), “Since she is not included in ‘arise, eat matza,’ she is not included in ‘you shall not eat leaven,’” it relies on what we derive “fifteenth, fifteenth” from the Festival of Sukkot, where “the native” is written, to exclude women. And if you say: then let us say that since they are included in [the prohibition of] wearing sha’atnez, they are included in twisted cords! One may answer: on the contrary, the whole Torah is juxtaposed to phylacteries [from which women are exempt]. And if you say: so too regarding matza [it should be juxtaposed to phylacteries], he answered: one can say that since they were included in [the prohibition of] eating leaven, they were included in eating matza.
rashi:b8.1: Since diverse kinds are permitted to them: at the time of service, since the belt was of diverse kinds, as it is written (Exodus 39:29): “And the belt of twisted fine linen [and blue and purple and scarlet]”; and since shesh [fine linen] is linen, the blue is wool, [as stated] in tractate Yoma (72b).
gershom:b7.1: [And these priests, since] diverse kinds were permitted to them, as it is written, “And the belt of twisted fine linen, blue and purple”; and since shesh is linen, the blue is wool.
tosafot:b9.1: Diverse kinds were permitted to priests at the time of service: since the belt was of diverse kinds, as it is written, “And the belt of fine linen,” and since shesh is linen, the blue is [wool], etc.
rashi:b11.1: That nothing may interpose between the priestly vestments and his flesh: and phylacteries must be on his flesh, under his garments, on the upper arm near the shoulder, as stated in Menaḥot, chapter HaKometz Rabba (37b), that they must be under his garments, as it is written, “It shall be a sign for you,” and not a sign for others. The frontplate rests on the forehead and the mitre on the head, and [the mitre] does not come down to the forehead; rather, the place of the phylacteries is visible at the top of the head, where a baby’s skull is soft.
tosafot:b11.1: That nothing may interpose between the priestly vestments and his flesh: and phylacteries must be on his flesh, as it is written (Exodus 13:9), “It shall be a sign for you,” and not a sign for others.
gershom:b8.1: “And the priest shall put on his linen garment [mido]” (Leviticus 6:3), and we say: “his garment [mido],” according to his measure [kemiddato], so that [the garments] must reach the joints of his fingers; and it is written “upon his flesh,” that nothing interpose between him and his flesh.
tosafot:b11.2: The frontplate rests on the forehead and the mitre on the head, and [the mitre] does not come down to the forehead; rather, the place of the phylacteries is visible at the top of the head, where a baby’s skull is soft; so [Rashi’s] wording. And one cannot ask why [the Gemara] does not say here, as above, “it teaches us that although they are exempt at the time of service [they are obligated otherwise]”: it is obvious to [the Gemara] that they are always obligated in the phylacteries of the head, and it had no need to say that one might think them exempt from the phylacteries of the arm when it is not the time of service, since it is obvious to it that they are obligated.
gershom:b9.1: His hair was visible between the frontplate and the mitre: evidently there was a free place [outside] the mitre to put the phylacteries there.
tosafot:b12.1: [Absence of the phylacteries of] the arm does not prevent [the mitzva of] the head: and although it is said elsewhere (Menaḥot 36a), “‘And for frontlets between your eyes’: as long as they are between your eyes, there shall be two,” that applies when one puts on both: he must put on the arm one first.
rashi:b15.1: “A day of sounding”: implies one day only.
tosafot:b15.1: “It shall be a day of sounding for you”: implies one day only.
rashi:b17.1: And to the blessings: since on Yom Kippur of the Jubilee Year they would also say [the blessings of] Malkhuyot, Zikhronot and Shofarot.
tosafot:b17.1: And to the blessings: since on Yom Kippur of the Jubilee Year they would also say Malkhuyot, Zikhronot and Shofarot.
rashi:b17.2: They sell at any time: even in the Jubilee Year itself, if they sold their land it is sold. Whereas of an Israelite it is taught in the Gemara of the last chapter (below, Arakhin 29b): “And in the Jubilee Year he may not sell, and if he sold it is not sold, and the money is returned.” And of priests we learned “they sell at any time”: it is sold, it goes out [at the Jubilee], and the money is theirs. For one cannot say that their land does not return at the Jubilee; it certainly returns, as it is written, “And if one of the Levites redeem” (Leviticus 25:33), and we say in the last chapter (29b): his sale goes out without payment.
tosafot:b17.2: In brief: Tosafot quote Rashi (a priest’s sale even in the Jubilee Year is valid, goes out at the Jubilee and the money is his) and reject it: Shmuel’s reason below (29b), that a field which is about to go out cannot be sold, applies to a priest as to an Israelite; and according to Rav, who says such a sale goes out, there would still be no difference between Israelites and priests regarding the Jubilee. They partly defend the reading from houses in walled cities: an Israelite may redeem those only within a full year, while Levites and priests redeem them at any time, and one might have thought their walled-city houses go out at the Jubilee like village houses; “sell” is mentioned only alongside “redeem.” They then quote Rashi in Rosh HaShana (29a), in the name of Rabbi Yitzḥak HaLevi: “they sell at any time and redeem at any time” are both mishnayot in Arakhin, taught in parallel to the rules for Israelites (who may not consecrate less than two years before the Jubilee, nor redeem less than a year after it). An Israelite who sells an ancestral field may not redeem it within two years (“according to the number of years of crops,” Leviticus 25:15–16), and one who sells a house in a walled city may redeem it only within a full year, while Levites redeem at once and at any time (“the Levites shall have a perpetual redemption”). And an Israelite who consecrated an ancestral field that the treasurer then sold loses it to the priests at the Jubilee, while Levites redeem at any time. So “they are not included in the mitzva of the Jubilee” here refers to that consecrated field: the Jubilee does not take it from a Levite as it does from an Israelite. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b10.1: And these priests, since they are not included in the mitzva of the Jubilee, as we learned in the last chapter of our tractate: the priests and Levites sell at any time, even in the Jubilee Year itself, and redeem even within two years, although it is written “according to the number of years of crops.”
